source: Chen et al. (2026) Practice Less, Explain More: LLM-Supported Self-Explanation in Calculus
finding: Randomised study (CMU) of three conditions: no explanation, menu-based, and open-ended explanation with LLM feedback. Ordinary post-test gains did not differ between conditions.
numbers: N=92 (Prolific; control n=29, menu n=35, open n=28). Gains: control +9.4, menu +5.9, open +9.3 points. Post-test ANCOVA: menu -2.4 (p=.564), open +0.8 (p=.842).
limits: Prolific adults, one calculus unit; one shared rubric; open condition also got feedback and a reference answer, so generation and feedback are confounded; probably underpowered.
agent_relevance: Explaining does not raise plain accuracy on familiar items. Do not expect a self-explanation step to lift ordinary solve rate.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Practice Less, Explain More
finding: Open-ended explanation with LLM feedback raised explanation quality on 'Not Enough Information' transfer items, though answer accuracy on the same items did not significantly rise.
numbers: NEI transfer explanation quality +11.9 points vs control (SE 5.8, p=.030, 95% CI 1.2 to 22.6, d=0.44). Combined open-ended transfer +7.3 (p=.057, d=0.38). NEI multiple-choice +9.3 (p=.183, d=0.26). Menu-based: +4.7 (p=.343).
quote: the open-ended condition produced significantly higher-quality explanations than control on NEI problems
limits: Only one of five outcomes crossed p<.05; no multiple-test correction reported.
agent_relevance: Effect lives in articulating what is missing or wrong, which matches S5 'name what is wrong'. Menu (pick from options) did not help: free generation plus a check mattered.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Practice Less, Explain More
finding: Time-cost finding: in a fixed 60-minute session the open-ended group did about a quarter of the practice problems yet gained as much as control.
numbers: Problems completed: control 58.9, menu 43.8, open-ended 16.9 (about 3.5x fewer). Gain +9.3 vs +9.4.
limits: Fixed-time design; authors say the earlier null results of Matthews and Rittle-Johnson (2009) and McEldoon et al. (2013) used unprompted explanations without feedback.
agent_relevance: Explaining costs several times more time per item. In an agent a naming step must be one line, or the budget cost cancels the gain.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Practice Less, Explain More (LLM grader validation)
finding: GPT-5.1 graded free-text explanations on a 4-level rubric about as well as humans agree with each other.
numbers: 160 explanations; two humans quadratic-weighted kappa 0.70; GPT-5.1 vs grader 1 0.68, vs grader 2 0.66, vs human consensus 0.78.
limits: One rubric and prompt for all items; consensus resolved by the first author.
agent_relevance: A model can score whether an explanation names the right principle if given a fixed rubric. Fits G5 only if scoring is rubric-based and sees no authorship cue.

source: Chen et al. (2026), citing Aleven and Koedinger (2002) and later dialogue tutors
finding: Older AI system: Cognitive Tutor geometry made students pick a principle (menu) after each step; later dialogue versions parsed typed explanations and gave corrective feedback. Read only as described in the 2026 paper.
numbers: Described: dialogue tutors needed hundreds of hand-written rules; 'equivalent learning with fewer practice problems'. Chen et al. say Aleven and Koedinger is the only earlier open vs menu comparison in ITS.
limits: Secondhand; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Earlier machine form of the method: explanation checked against a principle list. A code-side match to a known error class is the cheap analogue.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) Large Language Models are In-context Teachers for Knowledge Reasoning (Self-Explain)
finding: Model writes its own explanation for each training example, and those are used as few-shot exemplars. This beat human-written chain-of-thought exemplars on knowledge reasoning with GPT-3.5.
numbers: Test accuracy (MedMCQA / MedQA / StrategyQA): Human CoT 53.2 / 57.5 / 58.5; zero-shot CoT 52.5 / 55.2 / 52.7; Auto-CoT 53.1 / 55.6 / 56.1; Self-Explain 56.6 / 59.6 / 59.7. Text: about +2% over human CoT, about +4% with five sampled explanations per exemplar.
limits: GPT-3.5-turbo (0613) for the main table; row labels in the extracted table are ambiguous between plain and multi-explanation; knowledge QA, not maths.
agent_relevance: Own-voice explanations beat expert text as demonstrations. If the subgoal library stores worked examples, store the agent's own explained versions.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) In-context Teachers
finding: Correctness of the self-explanations barely mattered: explanations built from wrong answers worked about as well as right ones.
numbers: Right-answer explanations 56.6 / 59.6 / 59.7 vs wrong-answer 56.0 / 59.4 / 59.1 (MedMCQA / MedQA / StrategyQA).
quote: performance of prompting with self-explanation seems insensitive to its correctness
limits: Authors tie it to phrasing matching the model's training distribution, not logic; mechanism unverified.
agent_relevance: Warning: explanation text may act as a style cue, not as reasoning. Counts against trusting explanation content as evidence (G2, G3).

source: Zhao et al. (2024) In-context Teachers (Teach-Back)
finding: A student model is usually its own best teacher. Larger or stronger teacher models were not better. Aligning a small teacher to the student's own explanations closed the gap.
numbers: Table 3 (GPT-3.5 student): No CoT 41.1, human 55.6, Llama2-13B teacher 56.9, Mistral-7B teacher 53.5. Phi3-mini student: fine-tuned Mistral-7B teacher 59.3 (+4.9 over unfine-tuned Mistral, +1.6 over best unfine-tuned teacher). Abstract: about 5% over human teachers on medical QA. 94 to 98% of explanations passed their faithfulness filter.
limits: Medical and knowledge QA; small model set.
agent_relevance: Own explanations transfer best, which favours an agent keeping its own explained examples rather than importing another model's.

source: Lampinen et al. (2022) Can language models learn from explanations in context?
finding: Adding an explanation after each few-shot answer helped a 280B model on 40 hard BIG-bench tasks; the link between example and explanation mattered, since matched control explanations did not help.
numbers: Untuned explanations: benefit about one third of adding few-shot examples and about twice that of adding task instructions (log odds ratio / 1.81). Hand-tuned and selected explanations gave larger gains. Control explanations were neutral or harmful.
limits: Models up to 280B; only large models benefit, smaller ones did not; explanations placed after the answer.
agent_relevance: Explanation helps only when the model is large enough and the explanation is tied to its example. Test on our model before adding it.

source: Ye and Durrett (2022) The Unreliability of Explanations in Few-shot Prompting for Textual Reasoning
finding: Explanations in prompts gave small to moderate gains for most GPT-3-era models; only text-davinci-002 gained a lot. Generated explanations often did not follow from the input or prediction, yet could be used to flag bad predictions.
numbers: text-davinci-002 few-shot 72.0 / 77.7 / 69.1 vs explain-then-predict 86.9 / 82.4 / 75.6 and predict-then-explain 81.1 / 77.2 / 69.4 (three datasets). Calibrators built from explanation-reliability features improved accuracy on all three datasets.
limits: 2022 models; three text datasets; explain-first beat explain-after for the one model that benefited.
agent_relevance: Explanation consistency can be a cheap signal for a code check (does the explanation entail the answer), consistent with G5.

source: Gao et al. (2023) Self-Explanation Prompting Improves Dialogue Understanding in Large Language Models
finding: Zero-shot prompt asking the model to analyse every dialogue utterance before the task beat zero-shot CoT and plan-and-solve on six dialogue datasets with gpt-3.5-turbo.
numbers: MultiWOZ JGA: vanilla 35.93, CoT 27.64, plan-and-solve 39.19, self-explanation 44.44, with GPT-4 50.97. STARv2: vanilla 51.88, CoT 51.85, self-explanation 63.66 (about 12 point margin), GPT-4 70.27. MuTual: vanilla 68.97 vs 71.58 (GPT-4 91.87). MELD 59.14 vs 61.71.
limits: Comprehension tasks, not multi-step reasoning. Here 'self-explanation' means explaining the input, not a worked solution. Trigger wording mattered on MultiWOZ: 'understand' 36.52, 'summarize' 40.98, 'analyze each utterance' 44.44.
agent_relevance: Explaining the given context unit by unit is a distinct cheap operator. CoT hurt on MultiWOZ (27.64 vs 35.93), a warning against free reasoning.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion agents write a first-person verbal reflection on why a trial failed and store it in memory for the next trial. This is the closest deployed agent-loop form of 'explain what went wrong'.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. Gains over baseline: +22% AlfWorld (12 iterative trials), +20% HotPotQA, +11% HumanEval. Ablation on 100 HotPotQA questions: self-reflection gave about +8% absolute over episodic memory of the last trajectory alone.
limits: Needs an external signal (environment reward or unit tests).
agent_relevance: Direct support for S5: reflection on a real failure helps. Fits G2.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion (Rust ablation)
finding: Ablation on GPT-4 with the 50 hardest HumanEval Rust problems separated reflection from test generation.
numbers: Base 0.60; test generation without self-reflection 0.60; self-reflection without test generation 0.52; both 0.68. Internal-test false positive rate: MBPP Python 16.3%, HumanEval Python 1.4%.
limits: Small set (50 problems); one model.
agent_relevance: Self-explaining a failure with no executable evidence lowered accuracy by 8 points. Strong case for G2 and G3.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Rubber-duck step: model explains its code line by line, then uses explanation plus execution result as feedback. Explanation helped most when no unit tests exist.
numbers: Spider text-to-SQL: Codex baseline 81.3, simple feedback 81.3, +explanation 84.1; GPT-3.5 71.1 / 72.2 / 72.2; GPT-4 73.2 / 73.4 / 73.6; StarCoder 64.7 / 64.9 / 64.9. Abstract: +2 to 3% on Spider, +9% on hardest queries, up to +12% with unit tests on TransCoder and MBPP.
limits: Gain concentrated in Codex; near zero for GPT-4 and StarCoder on Spider. Code domains only.
agent_relevance: Explanation helps a weaker model and gives little to a stronger one. Re-measure on our model.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Self-Debugging (TransCoder table)
finding: On TransCoder, unit-test feedback did most of the work; adding explanation changed little and a line-by-line trace was worse.
numbers: Codex TransCoder: baseline 80.4, simple feedback 89.3, unit tests 91.6, unit tests + explanation 92.5, unit tests + trace 87.9.
limits: Column alignment read from a text extraction of the table; check the PDF before quoting precisely.
agent_relevance: Real execution output is the main signal; explanation is an add-on of about +1 point here.

source: Zelikman et al. (2022) STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning With Reasoning
finding: Rationalization: when the model gets a question wrong, give it the correct answer and ask it to explain backwards, then train on that. This is self-explanation of a known-correct answer used for learning.
numbers: CommonsenseQA: STaR with rationalization 72.5% vs without 68.8%; few-shot CoT GPT-J 36.6; direct fine-tuned 60.0; close to a 30x larger fine-tuned model (73.0%). +35.9 over few-shot baseline. Fraction of training set solved: 69.7% to 86.7% with rationalization.
limits: Uses weight updates, so training use does not transfer to our no-training agent; the inference-time lesson is hint-conditioned explanation.
agent_relevance: Explaining toward a known right answer is a worked-example step. Usable in our agent only when a verified answer exists (held-out or test-checked).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without external feedback, asking the model to review and fix its own answer lowered accuracy. With an oracle label it helped. The model cannot tell which of its answers is wrong.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic self-correction: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; HotpotQA 49 to 49 to 43. Oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, CSQA 89.7; GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5, HotpotQA 59.0. GPT-3.5 kept its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and more often changed right to wrong than wrong to right.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Two rounds; prompts taken from earlier papers; authors argue earlier positive results used oracle labels or weak initial prompts.
agent_relevance: Core rule: a naming step must be driven by a detected failure, never by self-judgment. This is G1 and G2.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Chain-of-thought explanations can rationalise a biased answer without naming the bias. Explanations look plausible but are not the true cause.
numbers: Accuracy dropped by as much as 36% on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks when the prompt biased the model toward a wrong answer (GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0).
quote: CoT explanations can be plausible yet misleading
limits: Older models; bias introduced via few-shot ordering and suggested-answer cues.
agent_relevance: An explanation is not a reliable trace. Treat it as a candidate label and check it with code (G2, G3).

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
finding: Tested truncating or corrupting the written reasoning and seeing whether the answer changes. Reliance on the stated reasoning varies by task, and larger models were less faithful on most tasks.
numbers: Interventions: early answering, adding mistakes, paraphrasing, filler tokens. Faithfulness got monotonically worse from 13B to 175B on several tasks; 13B most faithful on some. CoT gain not explained by extra compute or phrasing alone.
limits: Anthropic internal models of 2023; table numbers not extracted here.
agent_relevance: A larger agent model may write explanations it does not depend on. Test whether a revision changes the answer (mutation check) before crediting the explanation.

source: Oli, Banjade, Olney, Rus (2024) Can LLMs Identify Gaps and Misconceptions in Students' Code Explanations?
finding: LLMs critiqued student self-explanations of code (missing parts and wrong parts). GPT-4 with simple prompting beat LLaMA3 and Mistral; fine-tuning and preference optimisation (ORPO) beat prompting.
numbers: Dataset 2,888 simulated explanations (1,134 Java, 1,754 Python), 1,296 of them incomplete; split 75/20/5. Fine-tuned models up to 15% over simple prompting on gap detection; feedback quality up to 35% better after preference fine-tuning.
limits: Simulated student explanations (errors injected by program), not real students; introductory Java and Python code.
agent_relevance: A critic can say complete or incorrect but not which part is missing; see next line.

source: Oli et al. (2024) Gaps and Misconceptions in Code Explanations
finding: Prompted models invented problems in explanations that were correct, and could tell correct from incorrect but not locate the exact missing piece.
numbers: On complete and correct explanations the LLMs falsely flagged problems 27% of the time; on mostly correct explanations with small typos they invented non-existent issues in 34% of the qualitative sample.
limits: Qualitative sample, size not seen in the part read; temperature 0.
agent_relevance: A one-line 'what is wrong' from a model alone will over-flag. S5 should require a code-located failing output first (G2).

source: Lekshmi-Narayanan et al. (2024) Explaining Code Examples in Introductory Programming Courses: LLM vs Humans
finding: Compared GPT-3.5 line-by-line explanations of code with expert and student explanations. Only a search summary was read; the full text did not load (host unreachable).
numbers: Not read; per-metric scores unavailable.
limits: Secondhand from a search result summary.
agent_relevance: LLM can generate model self-explanations for worked code examples; whether it helps learners was not measured.

source: Engaging LLM to Explain Worked Examples for Java Programming: A Prompt Engineering Feasibility Study
finding: Search summary: GPT-4 explanations matched expert comments on clarity and step-by-step guidance, scored high on correctness, lower on completeness, conciseness and specificity. Not opened.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Secondhand; authors not verified.
agent_relevance: LLM-written explanations are correct but verbose and unspecific, the opposite of the one-line naming we want.

source: Oli et al. RCT on scaling self-explanation in programming with an intelligent tutor (par.nsf.gov 10561388)
finding: Search summary: randomised trial of 90 university students compared reading worked examples with scaffolded self-explanation in an automated tutor; low self-efficacy students learned almost twice as much interactively, a difference that was not significant. Page not fetched.
numbers: N=90 per the search summary; no further numbers.
limits: Secondhand; whether the tutor was LLM-based was not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: benefit may depend on learner profile; an agent has no equivalent, so note only.

source: Matthews and Rittle-Johnson (2009); McEldoon et al. (2013), as reported by Chen et al. (2026)
finding: Human boundary results as reported by Chen et al.: the self-explanation advantage disappears when controls get extra practice for the same total time, when explanations are unprompted verbal and have no feedback.
numbers: No numbers given in Chen et al.
limits: Secondhand; originals not opened (covered by other angles).
agent_relevance: Machine parallel: an explanation step must beat spending the same tokens on another attempt. Compare at equal token budget.

source: Gap: no direct LLM test of the Chi et al. (1989) mechanism found
finding: Across web searches and opened papers, no study was found that gives an LLM a worked example, makes it explain each step, and measures later problem solving. Nearest are Self-Explain exemplars, Lampinen explanations, Self-Debugging and Reflexion.
numbers: Zero direct hits in 4 web searches; arXiv API, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate limited.
limits: Search coverage partial; absence is not proven.
agent_relevance: Open test we could run ourselves: explained vs unexplained subgoal-library examples at equal tokens.

source: Synthesis across opened papers: explanation gains shrink as models get stronger
finding: Gains from explanation are large for weaker or older models and near zero for stronger ones, while very small models get no benefit (Lampinen). This gives an inverted U across model strength.
numbers: Spider: Codex 81.3 to 84.1 (+2.8), GPT-4 73.2 to 73.6 (+0.4). Ye and Durrett: only text-davinci-002 gained strongly. Lampinen: only large models gained.
limits: Cross-paper comparison on different tasks; descriptive, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Expect little from a naming step on a strong model unless a failure signal exists.
